items.followUp: Write two characteristics of kingdom Plantae.

rubric.why: One valid characteristic of fungi is required.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one accurate characteristic, such as being eukaryotic, lacking chlorophyll, having chitin cell walls, or being heterotrophic.

rubric.why: A second valid characteristic is required.
rubric.description: States a second characteristic of fungi.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a different accurate characteristic.

modelAnswer: They lack chlorophyll and have cell walls made of chitin.

items.followUp: Explain how cytokinesis occurs in animal cells.

rubric.why: Plant cytokinesis begins with the formation of a cell plate from vesicles.
rubric.description: Describes formation of the cell plate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Golgi vesicles gather and fuse at the equator to form a cell plate.

rubric.why: The cell plate grows across the cell and separates the cytoplasm into two daughter cells.
rubric.description: Explains how the cell plate completes division.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the plate grows outward to join the cell wall and divides the cytoplasm.

modelAnswer: Golgi vesicles gather at the equator of the plant cell and fuse to form a cell plate.
The cell plate grows outward until it joins the cell wall, separating the cytoplasm into two daughter cells.

items.followUp: What is cancer, and how can it develop?

rubric.why: A tumor is an abnormal mass or growth of cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a tumor as an abnormal mass or growth of cells.

rubric.why: Tumors develop when cell division becomes uncontrolled, often following changes in cell-cycle control.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking tumor formation to uncontrolled cell division or growth, or to mutations disrupting cell-cycle control.

modelAnswer: A tumor is an abnormal mass of cells.
It forms when cells divide uncontrollably, often because mutations disrupt the normal control of the cell cycle.

items.followUp: Compare aerobic respiration with anaerobic respiration in yeast.

rubric.why: Alcoholic fermentation produces ethanol and carbon dioxide, commonly in yeast.
rubric.description: States the products of alcoholic fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying ethanol and carbon dioxide as its products.

rubric.why: Lactic acid fermentation produces lactic acid rather than ethanol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.description: States the product of lactic acid fermentation and distinguishes it from alcoholic fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying lactic acid as the product; accept mention of muscle cells or bacteria as the site.

modelAnswer: Alcoholic fermentation, commonly carried out by yeast, produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Lactic acid fermentation, which occurs in some bacteria and in muscle cells, produces lactic acid.

items.followUp: How does carbon dioxide concentration affect the rate of photosynthesis?

rubric.why: Increasing light intensity generally increases the rate of photosynthesis when light is limiting.
rubric.description: States the effect of increasing light intensity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking greater light intensity with a higher photosynthesis rate, or low light with a low rate.

rubric.why: The rate eventually levels off when another factor becomes limiting or the light response reaches saturation.
rubric.description: Describes the limit to the effect of light intensity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rate stops increasing at high intensity because another factor becomes limiting or the rate reaches saturation.

modelAnswer: As light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases while light is a limiting factor.
At high light intensity, the rate levels off because another factor becomes limiting.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a cofactor and a coenzyme.

rubric.why: A prosthetic group is a non-protein component tightly associated with an enzyme and needed for its activity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as a non-protein component tightly bound to an enzyme.

rubric.why: A metabolic pathway is a sequence of enzyme-catalysed reactions that converts starting substances into products.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a metabolic pathway as a series of linked chemical reactions, usually catalysed by enzymes.

modelAnswer: A prosthetic group is a non-protein component that is tightly bound to an enzyme and is needed for its activity.
A metabolic pathway is a series of linked, enzyme-catalysed reactions that converts a starting substance into products.

items.followUp: Define digestion and explain how it differs from absorption.

rubric.why: Assimilation is the use or incorporation of absorbed nutrients into the body's cells and tissues.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for explaining that absorbed food or nutrients are incorporated into body material, used to build tissues, or used by cells.

modelAnswer: Assimilation is the process by which absorbed nutrients are incorporated into body cells and used to build tissues or become part of the body's living material.

items.followUp: Differentiate between carbohydrates and vitamins as nutrients.

rubric.why: Nutrition is the process of obtaining and using food or nutrients for life and growth.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining nutrition as obtaining and using nutrients or food by an organism.

rubric.why: Macronutrients are needed in relatively large amounts, whereas micronutrients are needed in small amounts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the correct relative amounts required; examples such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats, or vitamins and minerals, may support the distinction.

modelAnswer: Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain and use food or nutrients for life and growth.
Macronutrients, such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats, are needed in large amounts; micronutrients, such as vitamins and minerals, are needed in small amounts.
